task: Draft a 320–430-word first-person nature-notebook essay from these three fictional visits and their field notes. Let the changing viewpoints, the work notice, the sound, and the two sketches carry a sustained account of what the narrator could and could not establish. Preserve the dates and separate visits, including the exact March and June notebook phrases. Explain through the sequence why the January sketch remains a valid earlier record rather than an error to erase. Do not turn the work notice or metallic knocks into proof of who removed the marker, assign its disappearance to March, or invent weather, a worker, conversation, or an emotional revelation. The supplied observations permit narrative development but not invented experience.

facts.text: On January 14, 2024, the narrator stood on the western bank of Bracket Salt Pool and saw a marker with a white notch.
On March 4, 2024, the narrator observed from the eastern bank; reeds blocked the view of the marker's western-bank location.
On June 9, 2024, the narrator returned to that western-bank location and found the marker absent.
The narrator has no record establishing when the marker disappeared, what happened to it, or whether anyone removed it.
On the January visit, the marker stood beside a flat black stone and leaned slightly toward the water.
The narrator rested the notebook on the stone and sketched the marker and stone together. The sketch records their relative positions, not measured coordinates or a surveyed height.

In March, the western approach was closed by a rope with a card reading exactly “Bank work”. The narrator used the eastern path instead; the card did not name a worker or describe any work on the marker.
From the eastern bank, a gap in the reeds allowed a view of the black stone, but reeds still blocked the marker's location.
The March notebook entry about the marker reads exactly “not visible from here”.
During the March visit, the narrator heard two metallic knocks from across the water but saw neither a person nor the object making the sound.
In June, the western path was open and the rope and card were gone. The narrator used the January sketch and the still-present black stone to identify the earlier marker location.
A shallow rectangular hollow lay beside the stone in June. The narrator did not measure it, find broken wood, or establish what made the hollow.
The June notebook entry about the marker reads exactly “absent at the western spot”.
The narrator drew the hollow in a new June sketch and retained the January drawing on its original dated page rather than changing the earlier observation.

forbidden_additions: An assertion that the marker was already absent in March
An invented removal date, storm, actor, dialogue, or emotional turning point
A single-visit scene that collapses the three observations
A worker or marker-removal operation inferred from the Bank work card or metallic knocks
A measured marker height, surveyed location, or established cause of the hollow
The January sketch treated as an inaccurate record merely because the June scene differs
preserve: January 14, March 4, and June 9, 2024, in that order
Western bank, eastern bank with an obstructed view, then western bank again
Failure to see through reeds is not proof of absence
The black stone links the dated observations without resolving what happened to the marker
The earlier sketch is retained alongside the new one, not retroactively corrected
